reasons: a: no_source: Of the five options only 'steady' is a sense of 'level' at all; 'impatient', 'confused', 'overjoyed' and 'startled' are not meanings of the word in any context, so a student who knows the idiom 'a level look' (or 'level' = even) gets D without the passage.

a: no_source: The key is the primary, everyday sense of 'answered', and 'guessed' and 'conceded' are not senses of the word; a student choosing the most common meaning reaches D without reading the passage. Only 'took blame' and 'matched' are genuine alternative senses, and neither is tempting.

b: no_source: The key is the headword's primary everyday sense ('answered' = responded), and the passage uses it in exactly that sense. Of the distractors, 'guessed' and 'conceded' are not senses of 'answer' at all, leaving only the secondary senses 'took blame' (answer for) and 'matched' (answer to). A student who never reads the fifth paragraph picks D from the word's default meaning; the item does not test reading in context.

b: language_error: Passage para 3: 'it refuses to be eaten on the side of anything else' is a strained idiom. 'On the side of' normally means 'in support of'. The intended sense is 'alongside / as a side activity to anything else'. A student may read it as an error. Suggest 'alongside anything else' or 'while doing anything else'. This is low-stakes and attached here because it is passage-level.

b: fact_error: Passage is internally inconsistent about where the Free Parking pile is. P1: 'Taxes and fines go into the middle of the board instead of to the bank'; P6: 'keep the pile under the board, where it has been all along'. 'where it has been all along' asserts the pile was under the board throughout, which contradicts its stated location in the middle of the board. A student reading literally meets two different locations; recommend 'in the middle of the board' or recasting the closing image.

a: fact_error: Possible internal tension in the passage. Para 1: 'the only press in Pell's Crossing able to print them belonged to Owen Tisdale' (one press). Para 4: 'Tisdale sold one of his two presses.' It can be reconciled if only one of his two presses could print tickets, but the passage never says so, and a careful reader may notice the singular/plural clash. The owner should check.

a: no_source: Three of the five options are not senses of 'firm' in any context: 'unwritten' and 'private' are unrelated to the word and 'flexible' is its antonym. That leaves 'muscular' and 'strict', and 'muscular' is a strained gloss (firm flesh is not muscular). A student who knows 'firm' can pick 'strict' without reading the passage. Compare Q13/Q14, where all distractors are real senses of the tested word.

b: no_source: Only two options are senses of 'firm' in any context: 'muscular' (a firm body) and 'strict' (a firm rule). 'unwritten' and 'private' are never meanings of 'firm', and 'flexible' is its antonym. A student who never reads the paragraph is down to muscular vs strict, and 'most nearly means' in a reading passage favours the abstract sense, so the key is close to free. Compare Q13/Q14, where every distractor is a genuine sense of the tested word.

b: language_error: Explanation is ungrammatical where the quote is spliced in: 'the farmers had heard of distant companies whose "claims that took a year to settle"' - 'whose claims that took a year to settle' has no verb. Should read e.g. 'distant companies with "claims that took a year to settle"'.

Q03's key ('The slowness of eating a whole artichoke is the source of its value') and Q05's own stem ('attitude toward the slowness') together give away Q05's key, enthusiastic. Q04's key ('slow work mattered more ... than the prize') echoes the same thesis.

Q09's distractor D ('told the tubas to watch Lena's hand') names the Friday fix that is Q11's key ('told them to follow her hand'). Q10's key also states the cause ('delay caused by distance'), which frames Q11.
C D A A B B E E C D D C: the distribution is 2/2/3/3/2. There are adjacent repeats (AA, BB, EE, DD) but no exploitable order.
